mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes E Class 250 CDI engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: Supply-only rebuilt OM651 engines range from £2,200 to £3,500 depending on engine code and condition. With specialist fitting, budget £2,600-£4,300 total. OM651.911 (E 250 CDI, 204 hp, 2009-2013): rebuilt £2,200-£3,200. OM651.924 (E 250 CDI 4MATIC / BlueTEC, 204 hp, 2011-2016): rebuilt £2,400-£3,500. Labour adds £400-£800 depending on specialist location.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of timing chain failure in an E Class 250 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cold-start rattle lasting 2-4 seconds is the classic early warning sign. If ignored, the chain can jump, causing limp mode, loss of power, and eventually catastrophic engine failure. Rattle on cold start that disappears after a few seconds. Metallic clanging sounds from the engine. Loss of power or limp mode (engine won't rev over 3,000 RPM). Timing chain replacement at a specialist costs £900-£1,500.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine on an E Class 250 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the car is otherwise sound. W212 E 250 CDI examples with good service history still command £4,000-£10,000 used, making replacement viable. A quality rebuilt OM651 costs £2,200-£3,500 supply only. The 250 CDI is the most powerful four-cylinder diesel in the range - desirable on the used market. A replacement engine with warranty costs less than financing a newer car. Specialist fitting adds £400-£800, not dealer rates of £1,500+.

mainEntity.name: What causes the OM651 timing chain to fail on E Class 250 CDI models?

acceptedAnswer.text: The OM651 uses a single-row timing chain mounted at the rear of the engine. Extended oil change intervals (over 10,000 miles) are the primary culprit. Stop-start systems accelerate wear. Chain stretch typically occurs between 50,000-120,000 miles. Cold-start rattle that disappears after a few seconds is the early warning. Full chain replacement at a specialist costs £900-£1,500. Some OM651 examples exceed 150,000 miles on the original chain with frequent oil changes.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the OM651.911 and OM651.924 engines in the E Class 250 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both are 2.1-litre twin-turbo diesels producing 204 hp and 500 Nm. The OM651.924 was introduced for 4MATIC (all-wheel drive) models and later BlueTEC emissions treatment. OM651.911 fitted to rear-wheel drive E 250 CDI BlueEFFICIENCY (2009-2013). OM651.924 fitted to E 250 CDI 4MATIC and BlueTEC models (2011-2016). Both share the same 83mm bore × 99mm stroke, 2,143 cc displacement. Both suffer from the same timing chain and injector seal issues.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Mercedes E Class 250 CDI engine last?

acceptedAnswer.text: With proper maintenance and 8,000-10,000 mile oil changes, OM651 engines regularly reach 200,000-300,000 miles. Some examples exceed 250,000 miles in taxi and fleet use. OM651 bottom ends are robust when properly maintained. Timing chain replacement at 80k-100k miles is recommended for peace of mind. Injector seal replacement at 60k-120k miles is key maintenance. Short oil change intervals (8k miles) are critical for timing chain life.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes Benz E Class 250 CDI - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The E 250 CDI badge represented Mercedes-Benz's high-output diesel offering across the W212 E-Class generation. Powered by the OM651 2.1-litre inline-four turbodiesel in twin-turbo form, it delivered 204 hp and 500 Nm of torque - making it the most powerful four-cylinder diesel in the E-Class range at the time.

milestones.description: **2009** - W212 E 250 CDI BlueEFFICIENCY launched with OM651.911 engine, 150 kW (204 hp), twin-turbocharged
**2009-2013** - OM651.911 fitted to rear-wheel drive E 250 CDI BlueEFFICIENCY saloon and estate
**2011** - E 250 CDI 4MATIC BlueEFFICIENCY introduced with OM651.924 engine, 150 kW (204 hp), permanent all-wheel drive
**2011-2015** - OM651.924 also fitted to E 250 CDI / BlueTEC 4MATIC models (212.082, 212.097)
**2014** - BlueTEC branding introduced on later E 250 CDI models with AdBlue emissions treatment
**2016** - W212 production ends; OM654 replaced OM651 in W213 generation

historyTimeline.closingNote: Every engine fitted to the Mercedes E Class 250 CDI is covered below, with UK rebuilt pricing and known failure points.

commonProblems.h2: Mercedes E Class 250 CDI Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The OM651 engine that powers the E Class 250 CDI delivers impressive performance - 204 hp and 500 Nm from just 2.1 litres - but the twin-turbo design and single-row timing chain create specific failure points. Timing chain stretch is the most significant concern, with injector seal failure ("Black Death") and oil cooler leaks also featuring prominently. Every rebuilt engine supplied through EnginesMarket includes upgraded components designed to address the original failure point, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited mileage warranty. Below, we break down what these failures cost to fix and when replacement is the smarter option.

problems.h4: Timing Chain Stretch - Why the OM651 in the E Class 250 CDI Fails Prematurely
problems.rootCause: The OM651 uses a single-row timing chain mounted at the rear of the engine. The chain stretches when oil change intervals exceed 10,000 miles - extended service intervals are the primary culprit. Stop-start systems accelerate wear. Cold-start rattle lasting 2-4 seconds is the classic early warning sign.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replacement of timing chain tensioner only
repairOptions.longevity: 50,000-80,000 miles; effective if rattle is brief (under 2 seconds) and chain has not stretched

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replacement of timing chain, tensioner, guides and sprockets
repairOptions.longevity: When chain has stretched or rattle persists beyond start-up

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit of rebuilt OM651 with new timing components and upgraded parts
repairOptions.longevity: When chain has jumped and bent valves, or engine has suffered consequential damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical W212 E Class 250 CDI is worth £4,000-£10,000 depending on condition and mileage【INDUSTRY ESTIMATE】. Given the strong residual value of the 250 CDI (the most powerful four-cylinder diesel in the range), a rebuilt engine with warranty is usually justifiable if the rest of the car is sound.
problems.recommendation: The cold-start rattle is your early warning - don't ignore it. A specialist timing chain replacement at £900-£1,500 is significantly cheaper than the £2,000+ valvetrain rebuild if the chain jumps. Given the OM651's single-row chain design, preventative replacement at 80,000-100,000 miles is a wise investment on a high-value E 250 CDI. If the chain has already jumped, a rebuilt engine with upgraded components and warranty typically offers better value than a dealer-led rebuild.
problems.cta: -> Compare rebuilt OM651 Mercedes E Class 250 CDI engine prices

problems.h4: "Black Death" Injector Seal Failure - The OM651 Achilles Heel
problems.rootCause: The copper injector sealing washer degrades over time, allowing combustion gases to escape past the injector. This creates hard carbon deposits - the characteristic "Black Death" - that can weld injectors into the cylinder head. Early production OM651 engines (pre-2009) had faulty piezo injectors that were subject to a soft recall.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Removal of injectors, cleaning of injector bores, new copper seals and stretch bolts
repairOptions.longevity: 60,000-80,000 miles; effective if caught before carbon buildup becomes severe

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Stuck injector removal (may require specialist extraction tools), thread repair, new seals and injectors if damaged
repairOptions.longevity: 100,000+ miles; necessary when injectors are seized in the head

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit of rebuilt OM651 with new injectors, seals and upgraded components
repairOptions.longevity: When injector damage has compromised the cylinder head

problems.vehicleValueCheck: (Same as above - W212 £4,000-£10,000). If the vehicle is worth under £4,000, a used engine or minor injector seal repair is usually the pragmatic choice. For cars worth £5,000+, a rebuilt engine with warranty can be justified if the rest of the car is sound.
problems.recommendation: Injector seal replacement is almost always the right first step if caught early - the £350-£550 specialist cost is far less than the £2,000+ bill for a seized injector removal and head repair. If "Black Death" has been ignored and the injectors are seized, weigh the cost of head repair against a rebuilt engine. On a W212 E 250 CDI with good bodywork and transmission, a rebuilt engine often makes more sense than a costly extraction job.
problems.cta: -> Get OM651 Mercedes E Class 250 CDI injector seal quotes

problems.group: Oil Cooler & Oil Filter Housing Leaks
problems.h4: Oil Cooler & Oil Filter Housing Leaks - The OM651 Weeping Problem
problems.rootCause: The OM651's oil cooler seals and oil filter housing gaskets degrade with heat cycles, causing external oil leaks. These leaks can be minor drips initially but worsen over time, potentially leading to oil starvation if left unaddressed.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replacement of oil cooler seals, clean-up of oil residue

repairOptions.tier: Intermediate - Oil Filter Housing & Cooler Seals
repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replacement of oil filter housing gasket and oil cooler seals together
repairOptions.longevity: 100,000+ miles; addresses multiple common leak points

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit of rebuilt OM651 with new seals and gaskets
repairOptions.longevity: When oil loss has caused bearing damage or engine failure

problems.vehicleValueCheck: (Same as above - W212 £4,000-£10,000). On cars worth over £5,000, addressing oil leaks promptly prevents more serious damage.
problems.recommendation: Oil cooler seal replacement is a relatively straightforward job at a specialist. Don't ignore oil drips - they can lead to turbocharger oil starvation and catastrophic failure. If caught early, the £300-£500 specialist fix is excellent value. If oil loss has already caused bearing damage, a rebuilt engine is the only safe option.
